chunk_findings.detail: The entry declares `"mcp.tools": ("all", "no safety dimension; every tool advertised, as without the knob")`. `mcp.tools` controls which MCP tools are advertised to a client, which is a capability/safety control, not a knob with "no safety dimension". Because the fallback is applied to *unknown* file values, the scenario the invariant promises to protect against is exactly the one that breaks here: a config file that deliberately tightens `mcp.tools` to a restricted value but contains a typo (e.g. whatever the restrictive enum member is, mistyped) is tolerated and then resolved to `"all"` — every tool, including mutating ones, is exposed. That is a quiet loosening of a deliberately tightened setting, directly contradicting the stated rule that a typo "can only make ddflow more careful, never quietly loosen it." The strictest fallback for this knob must be the most restrictive member of its choice set (the one advertising the fewest tools), not the default `"all"`. The rationale string itself concedes `"all"` is the pre-knob/default behaviour, which is the criterion the change reserves for knobs with *no* safety dimension.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_forget_fallback` rewrites an entry only when it still contains the literal mark `" (not a value this ddflow knows; in effect: "`, but the rewrite it produces ("… overridden by the {source} value {value!r})") *removes* that mark. So the note can be corrected at most once: once one layer overrides a fallback note, a second, later layer that sets the same key can no longer update it, and the note keeps naming a value that is no longer in effect.

Concrete input (env is applied after local, as the highest-precedence layer — the same ordering that makes the new `test_an_env_value_overrides_a_bad_file_value_and_the_note_says_so` pass):
- `.ddflow/config.toml`: `[enforce]\nstale_docs = "blok"` → fallback note is appended, value `block`.
- `.ddflow/local/config.toml`: `[enforce]\nstale_docs = "warn"` → valid, so the note is rewritten to `enforce.stale_docs = 'blok' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the local value 'warn')`, mark gone.
- env `DDFLOW_ENFORCE_STALE_DOCS=off` → valid, `_forget_fallback` finds no entry containing the mark, so it does nothing.

Result: `cfg.enforce.stale_docs == "off"` and `cfg.sources["enforce.stale_docs"] == "env"`, but the sole `unknown_knobs` entry still says the file value was overridden by the *local* value `'warn'` and never names `'off'`. That is exactly the failure the docstring is trying to prevent ("doctor reports `block` while `warn` runs") — doctor here reports `warn` while `off` runs. The fix would need to match/update the note without depending on the mark surviving a prior rewrite (or track the fallback entry separately).

chunk_findings.detail:
`_forget_fallback` reconstructs the note by splitting the stored entry on the literal delimiter `" (not a value this ddflow knows; "` (`entry.split(mark)[0]`). That entry was built with the user's bad value interpolated via `bad!r`, so the delimiter can occur inside the value, and `split` will then cut at the wrong occurrence and truncate the repr.

Concrete input: a config file containing

    [ci]
    on_merge = "a (not a value this ddflow knows; b"

with a later layer (e.g. `DDFLOW_CI_ON_MERGE`/`--set`) setting `ci.on_merge = "off"`. During the file load the fallback entry is

    ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; b' (not a value this ddflow knows; in effect: 'full', the strictest)

and when the later layer sets the key, `entry.split(mark)[0]` stops at the delimiter embedded in the *bad value*, producing

    ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the environment value 'off')

i.e. an unbalanced quote and a note that no longer contains the offending value, instead of a well-formed `ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; b' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by ...)`.

This is not just formatting: the diagnostic that the whole method exists to maintain (`unknown_knobs`, shown by `doctor`) is silently corrupted whenever a tolerated bad value contains the fixed marker phrase. The runtime value is unaffected, so severity is low, but the note-surgery should key off the entry prefix/known layout rather than splitting on a delimiter that is attacker/user-controlled data.

chunk_findings.detail: The invalid-value branch now calls `self._forget_fallback(f"{sec}.{knob}", source, bad)` with the *rejected* value, whereas the pre-change code passed `value`, i.e. the strictest fallback that is actually put into effect. `_fallback_notes` may hold a note from an earlier tolerated layer for the same key (the comment and the `_apply(values, lenient, source)` signature make multi-layer application the normal case), and `_forget_fallback` rewrites that note to `"{key} = 'bad1' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the {source} value 'bad2')"`. But `bad2` is itself rejected: the value that takes effect for the knob is the strictest one (`block`/the refusing value), not `bad2`. So doctor ends up naming a value that is not running, which is precisely the failure `_forget_fallback` exists to prevent (its own docstring: “or doctor reports `block` while `warn` runs”), and it contradicts the stated requirement that the note “names the value in effect.” Concretely: layer A sets `enforce.stale_docs = 'bogusA'` and layer B sets `enforce.stale_docs = 'bogusB'`; A’s note becomes `enforce.stale_docs = 'bogusA' (… overridden by the config value 'bogusB')` while `block` is what actually runs. Passing the strictest `value` (as before) avoids this; alternatively drop the note rather than attributing it to a value that was discarded.

chunk_findings.detail: `_while_live` treats its `check` as safe to discard and re-run, but the first caller passes `sc.ddflow("claim", "P1.T1", agent="epsilon", ...)`, and a claim is a state mutation, not an observation. The retry branch is entered exactly when `done - renewed >= TTL_S`, i.e. when the subprocess returned after the 8 s lease measured from the heartbeat. On the loaded host this code exists for (the docstring itself targets load average 100–190), the `ddflow` process can start cheaply but reach the server *after* `renewed + TTL_S`; at that point the lease has expired, epsilon's claim is no longer "refused", and epsilon becomes the holder of `P1.T1`. The function discards that result as "ran too late" and loops; the next iteration runs `sc.ddflow("heartbeat", "P1.T1", agent="delta")`, which is not the holder, so nothing re-establishes DELTA's lease, and `lease = sc.jddflow("show", "P1.T1")["lease"]` then reports `holder == "epsilon"`. The very next statement, `sc.check("the live lease is DELTA's", lease["holder"] == "delta", ...)`, fails, and the scenario aborts with a misleading failure instead of either passing or failing on the intended `code == 3`. The original single-shot code failed too in that environment, but it failed on the assertion it was checking; the new retry cannot recover, because the mutation it caused is never undone (and epsilon's seized lease also poisons the later `recover` observation). A re-runnable check must be side-effect free (like the asserted read-only `recover`), or the claim result must not be discarded once it has been applied.

chunk_findings.detail:
The earlier layer's strictest-fallback note is now rewritten so that it names the current layer's *raw, rejected* value rather than the value that is actually in effect. The `_fallback_notes` structure is a `dict[str, list[tuple[int, str]]]` and is appended to on every bad value, so it exists precisely because the same key can accumulate more than one fallback note (two config layers both supplying an invalid value for the same knob). Concretely, with a lower-priority file layer setting `enforce.stale_docs = 'nope'` (falls back to `'block'`) and a higher-priority file layer setting `enforce.stale_docs = 'wrong'` (also falls back to `'block'`), the lower note becomes:

    enforce.stale_docs = 'nope' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the project file value 'wrong')

But `'wrong'` was itself rejected and never became the value in effect — the value in effect is still `'block'`, and the higher layer's own note (`… in effect: 'block', the strictest`) says so. Doctor therefore emits a note that names a value not in effect, contradicting the stated requirement that the doctor note name the value in effect. The previous code passed the resolved `value` (the strictest), which named the value actually in effect; the change to `bad` is what introduces the misreport. The comment justifying the change ("an earlier layer's note names what THIS layer wrote") does not hold when the current layer's value is bad, because a bad value does not override anything — it is discarded in favour of the strictest fallback.

chunk_findings.detail: `_while_live` re-runs `check()` after a fresh heartbeat whenever the previous attempt *finished* past `renewed + TTL_S`, but both callbacks it is used with change state precisely on that path. The `recover` callback is the clearest case: while the lease is live it returns 2 (read-only), but if it finishes after the lease could have expired — the only case that triggers the retry — it has performed its job (recovered the crashed P1.T1) and the task is no longer DELTA's. chunk_findings.detail: `_while_live` treats its `check` as safe to discard and re-run, but the first caller passes `sc.ddflow("claim", "P1.T1", agent="epsilon", ...)`, and a claim is a state mutation, not an observation. The retry branch is entered exactly when `done - renewed >= TTL_S`, i.e. when the subprocess returned after the 8 s lease measured from the heartbeat. On the loaded host this code exists for (the docstring itself targets load average 100–190), the `ddflow` process can start cheaply but reach the server *after* `renewed + TTL_S`; at that point the lease has expired, epsilon's claim is no longer "refused", and epsilon becomes the holder of `P1.T1`. The function discards that result as "ran too late" and loops; the next iteration runs `sc.ddflow("heartbeat", "P1.T1", agent="delta")`, which is not the holder, so nothing re-establishes DELTA's lease, and `lease = sc.jddflow("show", "P1.T1")["lease"]` then reports `holder == "epsilon"`. The very next statement, `sc.check("the live lease is DELTA's", lease["holder"] == "delta", ...)`, fails, and the scenario aborts with a misleading failure instead of either passing or failing on the intended `code == 3`. The original single-shot code failed too in that environment, but it failed on the assertion it was checking; the new retry cannot recover, because the mutation it caused is never undone (and epsilon's seized lease also poisons the later `recover` observation). A re-runnable check must be side-effect free (like the asserted read-only `recover`), or the claim result must not be discarded once it has been applied.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_forget_fallback` reconstructs the note by splitting the stored entry on the literal delimiter `" (not a value this ddflow knows; "` (`entry.split(mark)[0]`). That entry was built with the user's bad value interpolated via `bad!r`, so the delimiter can occur inside the value, and `split` will then cut at the wrong occurrence and truncate the repr.

Concrete input: a config file containing

    [ci]
    on_merge = "a (not a value this ddflow knows; b"

with a later layer (e.g. `DDFLOW_CI_ON_MERGE`/`--set`) setting `ci.on_merge = "off"`. During the file load the fallback entry is

    ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; b' (not a value this ddflow knows; in effect: 'full', the strictest)

and when the later layer sets the key, `entry.split(mark)[0]` stops at the delimiter embedded in the *bad value*, producing

    ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the environment value 'off')

i.e. an unbalanced quote and a note that no longer contains the offending value, instead of a well-formed `ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; b' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by ...)`.

This is not just formatting: the diagnostic that the whole method exists to maintain (`unknown_knobs`, shown by `doctor`) is silently corrupted whenever a tolerated bad value contains the fixed marker phrase. The runtime value is unaffected, so severity is low, but the note-surgery should key off the entry prefix/known layout rather than splitting on a delimiter that is attacker/user-controlled data.

chunk_findings.detail:
The earlier layer's strictest-fallback note is now rewritten so that it names the current layer's *raw, rejected* value rather than the value that is actually in effect. The `_fallback_notes` structure is a `dict[str, list[tuple[int, str]]]` and is appended to on every bad value, so it exists precisely because the same key can accumulate more than one fallback note (two config layers both supplying an invalid value for the same knob). Concretely, with a lower-priority file layer setting `enforce.stale_docs = 'nope'` (falls back to `'block'`) and a higher-priority file layer setting `enforce.stale_docs = 'wrong'` (also falls back to `'block'`), the lower note becomes:

    enforce.stale_docs = 'nope' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the project file value 'wrong')

But `'wrong'` was itself rejected and never became the value in effect — the value in effect is still `'block'`, and the higher layer's own note (`… in effect: 'block', the strictest`) says so. Doctor therefore emits a note that names a value not in effect, contradicting the stated requirement that the doctor note name the value in effect. The previous code passed the resolved `value` (the strictest), which named the value actually in effect; the change to `bad` is what introduces the misreport. The comment justifying the change ("an earlier layer's note names what THIS layer wrote") does not hold when the current layer's value is bad, because a bad value does not override anything — it is discarded in favour of the strictest fallback.

The new warning decides whether a bad entry *applied a fallback* or was *skipped* by substring-matching the human-readable note for the literal `" (not a value this ddflow knows; "`, instead of consulting the structured fallback bookkeeping (`_fallback_notes`) introduced with this feature. ```

the note for `enforce.not_a_knob (not a value this ddflow knows; x` matches `marker`, so it is classified as an applied fallback and the message prints `... ; each such knob takes the value named` while dropping the `, which this ddflow does not know; skipped` clause. The user is then told a nonexistent knob applied a value — exactly the false "it took effect" reading this change exists to eliminate. The same collision occurs for any skipped note whose rendered text contains that phrase (e.g. an unknown knob whose repr'd value contains it). Note that the added test cannot catch this direction of the mistake: it only asserts `"skipped" in err`, and that word still appears when the phrase is part of the embedded note. A membership check against the fallback-note map, or a structured flag per note, removes the ambiguity.

chunk_findings.detail: `_while_live` treats its `check` as safe to discard and re-run, but the first caller passes `sc.ddflow("claim", "P1.T1", agent="epsilon", ...)`, and a claim is a state mutation, not an observation. The retry branch is entered exactly when `done - renewed >= TTL_S`, i.e. when the subprocess returned after the 8 s lease measured from the heartbeat. On the loaded host this code exists for (the docstring itself targets load average 100–190), the `ddflow` process can start cheaply but reach the server *after* `renewed + TTL_S`; at that point the lease has expired, epsilon's claim is no longer "refused", and epsilon becomes the holder of `P1.T1`. The function discards that result as "ran too late" and loops; the next iteration runs `sc.ddflow("heartbeat", "P1.T1", agent="delta")`, which is not the holder, so nothing re-establishes DELTA's lease, and `lease = sc.jddflow("show", "P1.T1")["lease"]` then reports `holder == "epsilon"`. The very next statement, `sc.check("the live lease is DELTA's", lease["holder"] == "delta", ...)`, fails, and the scenario aborts with a misleading failure instead of either passing or failing on the intended `code == 3`. The original single-shot code failed too in that environment, but it failed on the assertion it was checking; the new retry cannot recover, because the mutation it caused is never undone (and epsilon's seized lease also poisons the later `recover` observation). A re-runnable check must be side-effect free (like the asserted read-only `recover`), or the claim result must not be discarded once it has been applied.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new warning classifies entries by substring-searching the note text for the sentinel `" (not a value this ddflow knows; "`. But those note strings embed the user's own value (the field comment two hunks above says each note's parts are `"key = 'bad'"`), so the sentinel test is exactly the "parsing text that holds the user's own value" the removed comment said was forbidden. Given a config with a typo'd key under a known section:

```toml
[enforce]
stale_docs_typo = "x (not a value this ddflow knows; y"
```

the entry recorded in `unknown_knobs` is the note `enforce.stale_docs_typo = 'x (not a value this ddflow knows; y'`, which contains `marker`. Line 1813 therefore puts it in `fell_back`, and the emitted warning claims "...each such knob takes the value named" — i.e. that the knob took a strictest value and is in effect — when in fact this key is an unknown, skipped knob with no effect. The structural information needed to avoid this already exists in `_fallback_notes` (knob → note parts), so the fallback/skipped split should be driven by that mapping rather than by matching a sentinel against user-controlled text. This only misleads the diagnostic (the applied value is unaffected), hence LOW, but it inverts the very distinction this change is meant to make.

chunk_findings.detail: `dataclasses.replace(cfg)` performs a shallow copy: the returned instance is constructed by passing the *same object references* for every init field to the new `__init__`. So `copy.unknown_knobs`, `copy._fallback_notes`, and `copy.sources` are the very same list/dict objects held by `cfg`. The test then calls `copy._apply({"enforce": {"stale_docs": "warn"}}, "env")`, which — for the fallback note to stop being reported, as the assertion requires — must remove or rewrite the entry inside those shared containers. That mutation is therefore also applied to the original `cfg` that the test goes on to inspect (`cfg.as_dict()`, `cfg._sections()`), and more importantly it means the entry at `copy.unknown_knobs[0]` is the shared fallback entry, not a copy-specific one. Concretely: if `_apply` drops the stale entry (the natural reading of an env override that replaces the file fallback), `copy.unknown_knobs` becomes empty and `copy.unknown_knobs[0]` raises `IndexError`, so the test errors instead of validating anything; if it merely rewrites the entry, the assertion `"in effect" not in copy.unknown_knobs[0]` is checking state that `dataclasses.replace` did not isolate. Either way the test cannot distinguish “`replace` carried the fallback notes” (its title) from “the notes were dropped by `replace`”, because the only object it inspects is shared with `cfg`. To actually exercise the property the title claims, the copy must be made independent of `cfg` (deep copy of the note containers) or `_apply` must be invoked on a config that shares nothing with the fixture.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_forget_fallback` reconstructs the note by splitting the stored entry on the literal delimiter `" (not a value this ddflow knows; "` (`entry.split(mark)[0]`). That entry was built with the user's bad value interpolated via `bad!r`, so the delimiter can occur inside the value, and `split` will then cut at the wrong occurrence and truncate the repr.

Concrete input: a config file containing

    [ci]
    on_merge = "a (not a value this ddflow knows; b"

with a later layer (e.g. `DDFLOW_CI_ON_MERGE`/`--set`) setting `ci.on_merge = "off"`. During the file load the fallback entry is

    ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; b' (not a value this ddflow knows; in effect: 'full', the strictest)

and when the later layer sets the key, `entry.split(mark)[0]` stops at the delimiter embedded in the *bad value*, producing

    ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the environment value 'off')

i.e. an unbalanced quote and a note that no longer contains the offending value, instead of a well-formed `ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; b' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by ...)`.

This is not just formatting: the diagnostic that the whole method exists to maintain (`unknown_knobs`, shown by `doctor`) is silently corrupted whenever a tolerated bad value contains the fixed marker phrase. The runtime value is unaffected, so severity is low, but the note-surgery should key off the entry prefix/known layout rather than splitting on a delimiter that is attacker/user-controlled data.

chunk_findings.detail:
The earlier layer's strictest-fallback note is now rewritten so that it names the current layer's *raw, rejected* value rather than the value that is actually in effect. The `_fallback_notes` structure is a `dict[str, list[tuple[int, str]]]` and is appended to on every bad value, so it exists precisely because the same key can accumulate more than one fallback note (two config layers both supplying an invalid value for the same knob). Concretely, with a lower-priority file layer setting `enforce.stale_docs = 'nope'` (falls back to `'block'`) and a higher-priority file layer setting `enforce.stale_docs = 'wrong'` (also falls back to `'block'`), the lower note becomes:

    enforce.stale_docs = 'nope' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the project file value 'wrong')

But `'wrong'` was itself rejected and never became the value in effect — the value in effect is still `'block'`, and the higher layer's own note (`… in effect: 'block', the strictest`) says so. Doctor therefore emits a note that names a value not in effect, contradicting the stated requirement that the doctor note name the value in effect. The previous code passed the resolved `value` (the strictest), which named the value actually in effect; the change to `bad` is what introduces the misreport. The comment justifying the change ("an earlier layer's note names what THIS layer wrote") does not hold when the current layer's value is bad, because a bad value does not override anything — it is discarded in favour of the strictest fallback.

chunk_findings.detail: `_while_live` re-runs `check()` after a fresh heartbeat whenever the previous attempt *finished* past `renewed + TTL_S`, but both callbacks it is used with change state precisely on that path. The `recover` callback is the clearest case: while the lease is live it returns 2 (read-only), but if it finishes after the lease could have expired — the only case that triggers the retry — it has performed its job (recovered the crashed P1.T1) and the task is no longer DELTA's. The loop's next iteration then heartbeats as `delta` and asserts `lease["holder"] == "delta"`; delta is no longer the holder, so the heartbeat fails (or the holder check fails), and the caller's `code == 2`/`code == 3` check is evaluated against a state it never intended to observe. The same applies to the epsilon `claim`: on the too-late path epsilon may have been granted the lease (the test exists precisely because the lease is live for the refusal, so past expiry the answer legitimately differs), which likewise makes the retry heartbeat/assertion fail and corrupts the subsequent steps of the crash-recovery scenario. Input that demonstrates it: a machine slow enough that the `recover`/`claim` invocation launched right after the heartbeat completes more than `TTL_S` later (the load conditions the docstring cites, ~100-190) — a timing retry that should re-observe the live window instead turns into a false failure because the retry does not restore the lease state (e.g. via an explicit release/re-claim as `delta`) before re-observing.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new warning decides whether a bad entry *applied a fallback* or was *skipped* by substring-matching the human-readable note for the literal `" (not a value this ddflow knows; "`, instead of consulting the structured fallback bookkeeping (`_fallback_notes`) introduced with this feature. The note embeds the knob's dotted key verbatim (the new test itself relies on `"enforce.not_a_knob"` being present in the note), so any skipped entry whose key text contains that phrase is routed into `fell_back`. Concretely, with a quoted unknown key:

```toml
[enforce]
"not_a_knob (not a value this ddflow knows; x" = 1
```

the note for `enforce.not_a_knob (not a value this ddflow knows; x` matches `marker`, so it is classified as an applied fallback and the message prints `... ; each such knob takes the value named` while dropping the `, which this ddflow does not know; skipped` clause. The user is then told a nonexistent knob applied a value — exactly the false "it took effect" reading this change exists to eliminate. The same collision occurs for any skipped note whose rendered text contains that phrase (e.g. an unknown knob whose repr'd value contains it). Note that the added test cannot catch this direction of the mistake: it only asserts `"skipped" in err`, and that word still appears when the phrase is part of the embedded note. A membership check against the fallback-note map, or a structured flag per note, removes the ambiguity.

chunk_findings.detail: The entry declares `"mcp.tools": ("all", "no safety dimension; every tool advertised, as without the knob")`. `mcp.tools` controls which MCP tools are advertised to a client, which is a capability/safety control, not a knob with "no safety dimension". Because the fallback is applied to *unknown* file values, the scenario the invariant promises to protect against is exactly the one that breaks here: a config file that deliberately tightens `mcp.tools` to a restricted value but contains a typo (e.g. whatever the restrictive enum member is, mistyped) is tolerated and then resolved to `"all"` — every tool, including mutating ones, is exposed. That is a quiet loosening of a deliberately tightened setting, directly contradicting the stated rule that a typo "can only make ddflow more careful, never quietly loosen it." The strictest fallback for this knob must be the most restrictive member of its choice set (the one advertising the fewest tools), not the default `"all"`. The rationale string itself concedes `"all"` is the pre-knob/default behaviour, which is the criterion the change reserves for knobs with *no* safety dimension.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_forget_fallback` rewrites an entry only when it still contains the literal mark `" (not a value this ddflow knows; in effect: "`, but the rewrite it produces ("… overridden by the {source} value {value!r})") *removes* that mark. So the note can be corrected at most once: once one layer overrides a fallback note, a second, later layer that sets the same key can no longer update it, and the note keeps naming a value that is no longer in effect.

Concrete input (env is applied after local, as the highest-precedence layer — the same ordering that makes the new `test_an_env_value_overrides_a_bad_file_value_and_the_note_says_so` pass):
- `.ddflow/config.toml`: `[enforce]\nstale_docs = "blok"` → fallback note is appended, value `block`.
- `.ddflow/local/config.toml`: `[enforce]\nstale_docs = "warn"` → valid, so the note is rewritten to `enforce.stale_docs = 'blok' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the local value 'warn')`, mark gone.
- env `DDFLOW_ENFORCE_STALE_DOCS=off` → valid, `_forget_fallback` finds no entry containing the mark, so it does nothing.

Result: `cfg.enforce.stale_docs == "off"` and `cfg.sources["enforce.stale_docs"] == "env"`, but the sole `unknown_knobs` entry still says the file value was overridden by the *local* value `'warn'` and never names `'off'`. That is exactly the failure the docstring is trying to prevent ("doctor reports `block` while `warn` runs") — doctor here reports `warn` while `off` runs. The fix would need to match/update the note without depending on the mark surviving a prior rewrite (or track the fallback entry separately).

chunk_findings.detail: The invalid-value branch now calls `self._forget_fallback(f"{sec}.{knob}", source, bad)` with the *rejected* value, whereas the pre-change code passed `value`, i.e. the strictest fallback that is actually put into effect. `_fallback_notes` may hold a note from an earlier tolerated layer for the same key (the comment and the `_apply(values, lenient, source)` signature make multi-layer application the normal case), and `_forget_fallback` rewrites that note to `"{key} = 'bad1' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the {source} value 'bad2')"`. But `bad2` is itself rejected: the value that takes effect for the knob is the strictest one (`block`/the refusing value), not `bad2`. So doctor ends up naming a value that is not running, which is precisely the failure `_forget_fallback` exists to prevent (its own docstring: “or doctor reports `block` while `warn` runs”), and it contradicts the stated requirement that the note “names the value in effect.” Concretely: layer A sets `enforce.stale_docs = 'bogusA'` and layer B sets `enforce.stale_docs = 'bogusB'`; A’s note becomes `enforce.stale_docs = 'bogusA' (… overridden by the config value 'bogusB')` while `block` is what actually runs. Passing the strictest `value` (as before) avoids this; alternatively drop the note rather than attributing it to a value that was discarded.

chunk_findings.detail: `_warn_unknown` now partitions `unknown_knobs` into "fallback" vs "skipped" solely by membership in `cfg.fallback_entries()`, but `fallback_entries()` is computed on the *post-apply* config, and `_forget_fallback` (invoked by `_apply`, as the changed test itself exercises with `copy._apply({"enforce": {"stale_docs": "warn"}}, "env")`) drops the note for any knob a later layer set, while the corresponding entry stays in `unknown_knobs` (the test asserts `copy.unknown_knobs[0].endswith("overridden by the env value 'warn')")`). So for a config file containing `[enforce]\nstale_docs = "blok"` loaded with an env layer that sets `stale_docs = "warn"`, `load()` runs file-apply (creates the note at index 0), env-apply (`_forget_fallback` rewrites `unknown_knobs[0]` to `enforce.stale_docs = 'blok' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the env value 'warn')` and removes the note), then calls `_warn_unknown(cfg.unknown_knobs, root, cfg.fallback_entries())` with an empty `fallbacks`. The entry therefore lands in `skipped` and stderr reads `enforce.stale_docs = 'blok' (... overridden by the env value 'warn'), which this ddflow does not know; skipped` — a known enum knob reported as "this ddflow does not know; skipped" even though the same entry text says its value was overridden by the env layer. The binary partition assumes every `unknown_knobs` entry is either an applied strictest-fallback or an unknown key, but an overridden fallback is a third state that the text-based classification happened to route to the fallback branch; the bookkeeping-based classification routes it to the wrong branch. (If `_forget_fallback` leaves the note in place instead of removing it, the same override is instead mis-reported as still taking the strictest value, e.g. `takes the value 'block'` while `warn` is in effect — either way the override case is mislabeled.)

chunk_findings.detail: The entry declares `"mcp.tools": ("all", "no safety dimension; every tool advertised, as without the knob")`. `mcp.tools` controls which MCP tools are advertised to a client, which is a capability/safety control, not a knob with "no safety dimension". Because the fallback is applied to *unknown* file values, the scenario the invariant promises to protect against is exactly the one that breaks here: a config file that deliberately tightens `mcp.tools` to a restricted value but contains a typo (e.g. whatever the restrictive enum member is, mistyped) is tolerated and then resolved to `"all"` — every tool, including mutating ones, is exposed. That is a quiet loosening of a deliberately tightened setting, directly contradicting the stated rule that a typo "can only make ddflow more careful, never quietly loosen it." The strictest fallback for this knob must be the most restrictive member of its choice set (the one advertising the fewest tools), not the default `"all"`. The rationale string itself concedes `"all"` is the pre-knob/default behaviour, which is the criterion the change reserves for knobs with *no* safety dimension.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_forget_fallback` rewrites an entry only when it still contains the literal mark `" (not a value this ddflow knows; in effect: "`, but the rewrite it produces ("… overridden by the {source} value {value!r})") *removes* that mark. So the note can be corrected at most once: once one layer overrides a fallback note, a second, later layer that sets the same key can no longer update it, and the note keeps naming a value that is no longer in effect.

Concrete input (env is applied after local, as the highest-precedence layer — the same ordering that makes the new `test_an_env_value_overrides_a_bad_file_value_and_the_note_says_so` pass):
- `.ddflow/config.toml`: `[enforce]\nstale_docs = "blok"` → fallback note is appended, value `block`.
- `.ddflow/local/config.toml`: `[enforce]\nstale_docs = "warn"` → valid, so the note is rewritten to `enforce.stale_docs = 'blok' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the local value 'warn')`, mark gone.
- env `DDFLOW_ENFORCE_STALE_DOCS=off` → valid, `_forget_fallback` finds no entry containing the mark, so it does nothing.

Result: `cfg.enforce.stale_docs == "off"` and `cfg.sources["enforce.stale_docs"] == "env"`, but the sole `unknown_knobs` entry still says the file value was overridden by the *local* value `'warn'` and never names `'off'`. That is exactly the failure the docstring is trying to prevent ("doctor reports `block` while `warn` runs") — doctor here reports `warn` while `off` runs. The fix would need to match/update the note without depending on the mark surviving a prior rewrite (or track the fallback entry separately).

chunk_findings.detail: The invalid-value branch now calls `self._forget_fallback(f"{sec}.{knob}", source, bad)` with the *rejected* value, whereas the pre-change code passed `value`, i.e. the strictest fallback that is actually put into effect. `_fallback_notes` may hold a note from an earlier tolerated layer for the same key (the comment and the `_apply(values, lenient, source)` signature make multi-layer application the normal case), and `_forget_fallback` rewrites that note to `"{key} = 'bad1' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the {source} value 'bad2')"`. But `bad2` is itself rejected: the value that takes effect for the knob is the strictest one (`block`/the refusing value), not `bad2`. So doctor ends up naming a value that is not running, which is precisely the failure `_forget_fallback` exists to prevent (its own docstring: “or doctor reports `block` while `warn` runs”), and it contradicts the stated requirement that the note “names the value in effect.” Concretely: layer A sets `enforce.stale_docs = 'bogusA'` and layer B sets `enforce.stale_docs = 'bogusB'`; A’s note becomes `enforce.stale_docs = 'bogusA' (… overridden by the config value 'bogusB')` while `block` is what actually runs. Passing the strictest `value` (as before) avoids this; alternatively drop the note rather than attributing it to a value that was discarded.

chunk_findings.detail: The new line is emitted unconditionally, but the promotion pipeline is only meaningful when `flow.environments` is set — the same change's own validation code (`pipelines(cfg, running=True)` in `ddflow/services/workflow.py`, with the comment "a project with no environments never runs the promotion pipeline, and a problem in it there would be noise") deliberately suppresses promotion concerns in that case. Concretely, for a project with `flow.environments` unset (a fresh init, or this repo), `WorkflowView.promotion_pipeline` is `list(cfg.gates.promotion_pipeline)`, so the command renders the line `A promotion passes through: ` with nothing after the colon (or, if a promotion pipeline was configured and environments were later removed, it advertises a pipeline that never runs). This is an empty/misleading output for the default case, and it is inconsistent with the gating the rest of this diff applies to the very same pipeline. The line should be conditional on the promotion pipeline actually running (or at least on it being non-empty).

chunk_findings.detail: `_while_live` treats its `check` as safe to discard and re-run, but the first caller passes `sc.ddflow("claim", "P1.T1", agent="epsilon", ...)`, and a claim is a state mutation, not an observation. The retry branch is entered exactly when `done - renewed >= TTL_S`, i.e. when the subprocess returned after the 8 s lease measured from the heartbeat. On the loaded host this code exists for (the docstring itself targets load average 100–190), the `ddflow` process can start cheaply but reach the server *after* `renewed + TTL_S`; at that point the lease has expired, epsilon's claim is no longer "refused", and epsilon becomes the holder of `P1.T1`. The function discards that result as "ran too late" and loops; the next iteration runs `sc.ddflow("heartbeat", "P1.T1", agent="delta")`, which is not the holder, so nothing re-establishes DELTA's lease, and `lease = sc.jddflow("show", "P1.T1")["lease"]` then reports `holder == "epsilon"`. The very next statement, `sc.check("the live lease is DELTA's", lease["holder"] == "delta", ...)`, fails, and the scenario aborts with a misleading failure instead of either passing or failing on the intended `code == 3`. The original single-shot code failed too in that environment, but it failed on the assertion it was checking; the new retry cannot recover, because the mutation it caused is never undone (and epsilon's seized lease also poisons the later `recover` observation). A re-runnable check must be side-effect free (like the asserted read-only `recover`), or the claim result must not be discarded once it has been applied.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new warning classifies entries by substring-searching the note text for the sentinel `" (not a value this ddflow knows; "`. But those note strings embed the user's own value (the field comment two hunks above says each note's parts are `"key = 'bad'"`), so the sentinel test is exactly the "parsing text that holds the user's own value" the removed comment said was forbidden. Given a config with a typo'd key under a known section:

```toml
[enforce]
stale_docs_typo = "x (not a value this ddflow knows; y"
```

the entry recorded in `unknown_knobs` is the note `enforce.stale_docs_typo = 'x (not a value this ddflow knows; y'`, which contains `marker`. Line 1813 therefore puts it in `fell_back`, and the emitted warning claims "...each such knob takes the value named" — i.e. that the knob took a strictest value and is in effect — when in fact this key is an unknown, skipped knob with no effect. The structural information needed to avoid this already exists in `_fallback_notes` (knob → note parts), so the fallback/skipped split should be driven by that mapping rather than by matching a sentinel against user-controlled text. This only misleads the diagnostic (the applied value is unaffected), hence LOW, but it inverts the very distinction this change is meant to make.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config.py:1812-1813 (marker / fell_back classification)

chunk_findings.detail: `dataclasses.replace(cfg)` performs a shallow copy: the returned instance is constructed by passing the *same object references* for every init field to the new `__init__`. So `copy.unknown_knobs`, `copy._fallback_notes`, and `copy.sources` are the very same list/dict objects held by `cfg`. The test then calls `copy._apply({"enforce": {"stale_docs": "warn"}}, "env")`, which — for the fallback note to stop being reported, as the assertion requires — must remove or rewrite the entry inside those shared containers. That mutation is therefore also applied to the original `cfg` that the test goes on to inspect (`cfg.as_dict()`, `cfg._sections()`), and more importantly it means the entry at `copy.unknown_knobs[0]` is the shared fallback entry, not a copy-specific one. Concretely: if `_apply` drops the stale entry (the natural reading of an env override that replaces the file fallback), `copy.unknown_knobs` becomes empty and `copy.unknown_knobs[0]` raises `IndexError`, so the test errors instead of validating anything; if it merely rewrites the entry, the assertion `"in effect" not in copy.unknown_knobs[0]` is checking state that `dataclasses.replace` did not isolate. Either way the test cannot distinguish “`replace` carried the fallback notes” (its title) from “the notes were dropped by `replace`”, because the only object it inspects is shared with `cfg`. To actually exercise the property the title claims, the copy must be made independent of `cfg` (deep copy of the note containers) or `_apply` must be invoked on a config that shares nothing with the fixture.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_config_enum_knobs.py:266 `test_replace_carries_the_fallback_notes`

chunk_findings.detail: `_warn_unknown` now partitions `unknown_knobs` into "fallback" vs "skipped" solely by membership in `cfg.fallback_entries()`, but `fallback_entries()` is computed on the *post-apply* config, and `_forget_fallback` (invoked by `_apply`, as the changed test itself exercises with `copy._apply({"enforce": {"stale_docs": "warn"}}, "env")`) drops the note for any knob a later layer set, while the corresponding entry stays in `unknown_knobs` (the test asserts `copy.unknown_knobs[0].endswith("overridden by the env value 'warn')")`). So for a config file containing `[enforce]\nstale_docs = "blok"` loaded with an env layer that sets `stale_docs = "warn"`, `load()` runs file-apply (creates the note at index 0), env-apply (`_forget_fallback` rewrites `unknown_knobs[0]` to `enforce.stale_docs = 'blok' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the env value 'warn')` and removes the note), then calls `_warn_unknown(cfg.unknown_knobs, root, cfg.fallback_entries())` with an empty `fallbacks`. The entry therefore lands in `skipped` and stderr reads `enforce.stale_docs = 'blok' (... overridden by the env value 'warn'), which this ddflow does not know; skipped` — a known enum knob reported as "this ddflow does not know; skipped" even though the same entry text says its value was overridden by the env layer. The binary partition assumes every `unknown_knobs` entry is either an applied strictest-fallback or an unknown key, but an overridden fallback is a third state that the text-based classification happened to route to the fallback branch; the bookkeeping-based classification routes it to the wrong branch. (If `_forget_fallback` leaves the note in place instead of removing it, the same override is instead mis-reported as still taking the strictest value, e.g. `takes the value 'block'` while `warn` is in effect — either way the override case is mislabeled.)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_forget_fallback` reconstructs the note by splitting the stored entry on the literal delimiter `" (not a value this ddflow knows; "` (`entry.split(mark)[0]`). That entry was built with the user's bad value interpolated via `bad!r`, so the delimiter can occur inside the value, and `split` will then cut at the wrong occurrence and truncate the repr.

Concrete input: a config file containing

    [ci]
    on_merge = "a (not a value this ddflow knows; b"

with a later layer (e.g. `DDFLOW_CI_ON_MERGE`/`--set`) setting `ci.on_merge = "off"`. During the file load the fallback entry is

    ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; b' (not a value this ddflow knows; in effect: 'full', the strictest)

and when the later layer sets the key, `entry.split(mark)[0]` stops at the delimiter embedded in the *bad value*, producing

    ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the environment value 'off')

i.e. an unbalanced quote and a note that no longer contains the offending value, instead of a well-formed `ci.on_merge = 'a (not a value this ddflow knows; b' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by ...)`.

This is not just formatting: the diagnostic that the whole method exists to maintain (`unknown_knobs`, shown by `doctor`) is silently corrupted whenever a tolerated bad value contains the fixed marker phrase. The runtime value is unaffected, so severity is low, but the note-surgery should key off the entry prefix/known layout rather than splitting on a delimiter that is attacker/user-controlled data.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config.py `_forget_fallback`

chunk_findings.detail:
The earlier layer's strictest-fallback note is now rewritten so that it names the current layer's *raw, rejected* value rather than the value that is actually in effect. The `_fallback_notes` structure is a `dict[str, list[tuple[int, str]]]` and is appended to on every bad value, so it exists precisely because the same key can accumulate more than one fallback note (two config layers both supplying an invalid value for the same knob). Concretely, with a lower-priority file layer setting `enforce.stale_docs = 'nope'` (falls back to `'block'`) and a higher-priority file layer setting `enforce.stale_docs = 'wrong'` (also falls back to `'block'`), the lower note becomes:

    enforce.stale_docs = 'nope' (not a value this ddflow knows; overridden by the project file value 'wrong')

But `'wrong'` was itself rejected and never became the value in effect — the value in effect is still `'block'`, and the higher layer's own note (`… in effect: 'block', the strictest`) says so. Doctor therefore emits a note that names a value not in effect, contradicting the stated requirement that the doctor note name the value in effect. The previous code passed the resolved `value` (the strictest), which named the value actually in effect; the change to `bad` is what introduces the misreport. The comment justifying the change ("an earlier layer's note names what THIS layer wrote") does not hold when the current layer's value is bad, because a bad value does not override anything — it is discarded in favour of the strictest fallback.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new summary line is appended unconditionally:

```python
f"A phase passes through: {', '.join(v.phase_pipeline)}",
f"A promotion passes through: {', '.join(v.promotion_pipeline)}",
```

while the rest of this very change establishes that the promotion pipeline only runs when `flow.environments` is set (the rewritten `findings()` comment: "a project with no environments never runs the promotion pipeline"; the `gates.required` message explicitly says so). `WorkflowView.promotion_pipeline` is filled from `cfg.gates.promotion_pipeline` regardless of `flow.environments`, so:

- Fresh init / any repo with no environments and no configured promotion gates: the command now emits `A promotion passes through: ` (a dangling empty list) where before there was no promotion line at all — output changes for every project even though no promotion pipeline exists or runs.
- A repo that has configured `gates.promotion_pipeline` but no `flow.environments`: the line advertises those gates as something a promotion "passes through", even though that pipeline is statically known not to run there. This is exactly the misleading/nonexistent-pipeline case the surrounding code takes care to exclude (`running=True`) and to explain in the `gates.required` finding.

The line should be conditional on the pipeline actually being relevant (e.g. emitted only when `cfg.flow.environments` is set / when `"promotion" in pipelines(cfg, running=True)`), matching the running-pipeline semantics used elsewhere in this change.

chunk_findings.detail: `_while_live` re-runs `check()` after a fresh heartbeat whenever the previous attempt *finished* past `renewed + TTL_S`, but both callbacks it is used with change state precisely on that path. The `recover` callback is the clearest case: while the lease is live it returns 2 (read-only), but if it finishes after the lease could have expired — the only case that triggers the retry — it has performed its job (recovered the crashed P1.T1) and the task is no longer DELTA's. The loop's next iteration then heartbeats as `delta` and asserts `lease["holder"] == "delta"`; delta is no longer the holder, so the heartbeat fails (or the holder check fails), and the caller's `code == 2`/`code == 3` check is evaluated against a state it never intended to observe. The same applies to the epsilon `claim`: on the too-late path epsilon may have been granted the lease (the test exists precisely because the lease is live for the refusal, so past expiry the answer legitimately differs), which likewise makes the retry heartbeat/assertion fail and corrupts the subsequent steps of the crash-recovery scenario. Input that demonstrates it: a machine slow enough that the `recover`/`claim` invocation launched right after the heartbeat completes more than `TTL_S` later (the load conditions the docstring cites, ~100-190) — a timing retry that should re-observe the live window instead turns into a false failure because the retry does not restore the lease state (e.g. via an explicit release/re-claim as `delta`) before re-observing.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new warning decides whether a bad entry *applied a fallback* or was *skipped* by substring-matching the human-readable note for the literal `" (not a value this ddflow knows; "`, instead of consulting the structured fallback bookkeeping (`_fallback_notes`) introduced with this feature. The note embeds the knob's dotted key verbatim (the new test itself relies on `"enforce.not_a_knob"` being present in the note), so any skipped entry whose key text contains that phrase is routed into `fell_back`. Concretely, with a quoted unknown key:

```toml
[enforce]
"not_a_knob (not a value this ddflow knows; x" = 1
```

the note for `enforce.not_a_knob (not a value this ddflow knows; x` matches `marker`, so it is classified as an applied fallback and the message prints `... ; each such knob takes the value named` while dropping the `, which this ddflow does not know; skipped` clause. The user is then told a nonexistent knob applied a value — exactly the false "it took effect" reading this change exists to eliminate. The same collision occurs for any skipped note whose rendered text contains that phrase (e.g. an unknown knob whose repr'd value contains it). Note that the added test cannot catch this direction of the mistake: it only asserts `"skipped" in err`, and that word still appears when the phrase is part of the embedded note. A membership check against the fallback-note map, or a structured flag per note, removes the ambiguity.
